newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU presents plans for "pig pullmans" for livestock.
newsitem.headline: EU presents plans for "pig pullmans" for livestock.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday put forward proposals for "pig pullmans" to transport livestock on long continental road journeys to fattening sites or abattoirs.

The proposals, which cover rules for animal bedding material, ventilation, watering and feeding in the vehicles, are intended to help put into force a 1995 agreement to protect animals taken long distances from northern to southern EU member states.

Southern countries, such as Italy, have complained have complained that the new rules will escalate costs, making the import of live animals uneconomic and throwing tens of thousands of people out of work.
But Britain and other northern countries, which export millions of farm animals annually, say that transport conditions are cruel.
"Every effort must be made to ensure that animal welfare considerations are fully taken into account," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in a statement.
But he added that it was up to EU governments to make sure that road haulage companies implemented and respected the rules.
The 1995 agreement set a basic eight-hour journey limit after which animals must be unloaded and rested for 24 hours.
Journeys could then be continued provided lorries met certain standards. Pigs could travel a further 24 hours provided that drinking water was constantly available.
A similar limit applied to horses which would also be fed every eight hours if necessary.
Cattle could be transported for another 14 hours after which they would be entitled to one hour's rest.
Piglets, lambs and calves, which were still being fed by their mothers, could travel an extra nine hours after which they would have an hour's break for watering and possible feeding.
Last month farm ministers agreed rules for "pig hotels" -- rest centres for farm animals during their long journeys.
